comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
We’ve been so fixated and obsessed on Law for so long, we can hardly think of any other way to run things, and not just governmentally. Policies and procedures, regulations, churches, businesses, fraternal organizations, academia, family rules… we’ve got the offspring of Law running all over us and coming out our ears.

So, you can guess what I think of “natural law”, “laws of nature”, “laws of science”, “laws of physics”, and the rest.

Show me a single person, anywhere, who recognized the possibility that “law” is nothing more than a metaphor erroneously affixed to real, observable patterns of behavior of physical phenomena and living beings, and show me any of those who did legitimate, intelligent work to rule that possibility out. 

Dare ya.

I’m tempted myself to talk that way, sometimes. To me, though, it’s like saying that person didn’t choose to follow their own consistent routines, but that they’ve got no choice about it, because a “law governs them” to consistently, routinely behave that way.

Makes sense as a theoretical possibility. Make no sense to say it’s real and true when you’ve got shitall facts or evidence that show it’s the only explanation, or that it’s the one which best fits the facts.

But if pattern in life approaches the qualifications to be regarded as a “law”, this one surely does. I’ll call it:

The “Law” of Freedom From Codependence”

It is my observation throughout my 70 years that, when it comes to things that really, really matter to us—the things that religious folks sweat drops of blood praying for, the things we feel like we’ll die without—we don’t get them until we reach a point where we’re just fine whether we get them or not. It’s so very weird.

You’ll be ready to do something when you’re just fine never doing it.

You’ll be ready to get something you wanted when you’ll be just fine whether you get it or not.

In other words, “ask, and you shall receive” is absolutely true, but it won’t come true until we emerge from our codependence on it.

What differentiates codependence from simple kinds of dependence like interdependence?

If you’re codependent, when faced with the fact that you can’t rely on what or whom seems to be your only hope, to you it will look and feel like the end of the world. “I’ll die if… [whatever]!!!”

If you’re dependent in a normal, healthy way, then when faced with the fact that can’t rely on what or whom seems to be your only hope, you won’t feel like you’re gonna die because:  

1) You know there might likely be other things you could rely on or other ways to meet the need which you can’t rely on others for anymore. It might not involve dependence at all.

2) You know that you can acquire the competence to deal with the need in completely different ways than you’re capable of now.

The sense I have, especially when it comes to the most important things, is that we’re not in a position to take care of what we want, navigate it and handle it properly, and be constructive instead of destructive, so long as we’re codependent.

comment.body:
Almost no one, anywhere, not even in academia, does this well. 

Validity" here is the philosophical term: only valid claims are candidates for judging how true or false they are. 

If your thinking tests high for bullshit, it means it's not even worth considering: not even in the running for "right"; not even wrong.

Take any chronically unresolved debate you like -- "theism vs. atheism", "nature vs. nurture", "determinism vs. free will", "chicken vs. egg"🤣--and do the checklist for both sides.

What will you find?

Both sides are bullshit.

In fact, were anyone to subject the complete corpus of academic thought to this checklist, they would find the same thing for the overwhelming majority of it.

The plain fact is that humans don’t know very much at all. If we did, we wouldn’t have made an Eden into such a hell as it is. And we wouldn’t make such a ridiculous to-do over what little we know.

comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
And this is far as I've seen anarchist thinking go. 

No concept of a culture which makes it a practical impossibility to concentrate power in the hands of the few, only for them to wield it against and at the expense of the many. 

Anarchists have all fallen to cultic capitulation: the key corruption of sound thinking that flips beliefs resistant to change into cultism.

Here’s how it works: a person, certain that something is true, having no facts or evidence and so blind in their belief that they can’t even tell themself why they believe it, refuses to find out if it might be a mistake. Instead, with all the certainty and confidence of someone who already made sure it’s not a mistake, they claim it's true in fact without ever noticing the circularity. Indeed, if you try to point out their circularity to them, you instantly become a threat—which is strange, because wouldn’t their certainty and confidence mean (if they were genuine) that their belief is unassailable?

So, instead of thinking systemically, anarchists, too, refuse the possibility of an asshole-resistant world and rest their hopes on hero saviors: developing a critical mass of self-thinking individuals that can eventually outweigh and eventually overcome in the perennial fight against evil statists, lol—”eventually” meaning so far ahead that it’s little more than fantasy for all present purposes. 

No wonder that anarchism, to date, has amounted to little more than talk.

comment.body:
I'm hugely supportive of your intent, Don. Don't get me wrong. But no one has even begun to start looking deep enough for what really needs to change and what the thermal exhaust port in this fucking Death Star actually is. 

"The public only has two tools of resistance… their labour and their money."

That's the problem right there: "only".

According to whom?

No question, that's the kind of thinking that the self-styled lords of "civilization" have spent quadrillions on what amounts to a millennia-long gaslighting project. "Only two tools: labor and money" come right out of the There-Will-Be-Rulers playbook.

No one is looking at the psychological dynamics involved. You've got to ask yourself what kind of terrified, deeply existentially precarious, supremely inferior kind of person needs to threaten everyone around them with harm to follow protocol, "law", ritual and the like to visibly signal obeisance? What kind of sick fucks need that **just to operate without meltdowns and hissy fits**?

We're not dealing with "superiors" here. We're dealing with the weakest of the weak that can't fathom what's the worst of all to their sorry asses: "chaos". The "chaos" of meeting other human beings on a fair footing without dictating the terms of engagement on pain of imprisonment, dismemberment, or execution.

We're dealing with psychotically delusional paranoids to whom everyone and everything is a "threat" until they've taken preemptive measures to "neutralize" it.

We've got *untold* numbers of tools in our hands. You don't need RPGs to take out flies.

Our problem is that we haven't sufficiently extricated our head out of the asses of the "rich and powerful" narratives. That needs to happen first before we'll realize the power and the riches are all ours. They just don't glint in the sunshine where everyone can see them -- which is yet another aspect of their infantilistic mentality.

Bluntly: we need to grow the fuck up and reject our own infantilism before we'll be in a position to act as anything more than the "bewildered herds" these debilitated shells of inhumanness make us out to be.
